message.content: In a world made of brushstrokes, the only real creature is the one that must keep its eyes from becoming paint. Nimbus was a hedgehog no bigger than a teacup, with glasses made from two curled twigs and a bridge of dried sap. Around him floated islands of color: a cobalt wave that sighed, a yellow triangle that hummed, a smear of magenta that stretched like a cat. There was no ground, only a pale grid of lines that seemed to mean “here” and “not here.” When Nimbus stepped, his claws made tiny, honest marks. The grid shivered. Reality, for Nimbus, was not the absence of abstraction but the ability to see where abstraction stopped. A tall ribbon of indigo asked him to become a line. “Be sharp,” it said, “and you will be beautiful.” A cluster of silver dots offered to be his eyes. “Be scattered,” they said, “and you will be everywhere.” Nimbus adjusted his glasses. The lenses were scratched, imperfect, real. Through them, the indigo ribbon looked cold and hungry; the silver dots looked lonely. “No,” he said, his voice like dry leaves. “I am here. I am small. I am not a shape yet.” The abstract forms learned to wait because one small creature refused to dissolve into their meaning. Over what might have been days, the world rearranged itself around him. The red circle began to orbit slowly, like a moon made of heat. The green slash softened at the edges when he passed. The gray fog gathered near his feet, curious. Nimbus did not command them. He simply blinked, sniffed the air, and moved from one color to another with the unhurried seriousness of an animal crossing a garden. One time, a black spiral threatened to swallow the light. Nimbus placed his nose against its edge. It recoiled, not from fear, but from the warmth of a heartbeat. A canvas can become a home when it contains a creature that asks what it wants to be. At the center of the abstract world stood a blank white square, the only place that seemed to remember silence. The shapes had tried to cover it: they painted, slashed, scattered, and framed it, but it always returned to emptiness. Nimbus carried a single quill that had fallen from his back. He pressed it into the square and drew a tiny circle. Then another. Then the outline of a face with two eyes and a small nose. The white did not become art exactly. It became a mirror. In it, the colors saw themselves reflected as they were—not beautiful, not true, but present. The only real creature does not rescue the abstract world; he teaches it that being real includes looking back. When the last shape settled into place, the world hummed like a held breath. Nimbus sat beneath the red circle, his glasses catching a flash of yellow. The cobalt wave rolled softly around him, not drowning him, only listening. The grid beneath his feet stopped meaning “here” and “not here.” It began to mean “where the hedgehog is.” And in that abstract place of impossible colors, something small and solid kept the universe company, one real blink at a time.
